title: The monastery hospital at Mihintale

traditional.note: The *Mahavamsa* chronicle credits King Pandukabhaya, who by its reckoning reigned in the 4th century BCE, with a lying-in house and a hall for the sick.

confidence.note: The ground plan of the Mihintale ruins, with rows of cells and a stone bath trough, is read as a monastic hospital; a university library's catalog dates it to the 9th century, while a site sign at Polonnaruwa calls the Mihintale design an 8th-century prototype. The far earlier royal hospitals rest only on a chronicle composed around 500 CE.

people: Pandukabhaya (4th century BCE by the chronicle's reckoning), king the *Mahavamsa* credits with a lying-in house and a hall for the sick
summary: A Buddhist hospital with cells for patients and a stone trough for medicinal baths — and a chronicle claiming hospitals 1,200 years older.
body: On the sacred hill of Mihintale, near Sri Lanka's ancient capital Anuradhapura, stand the ruins of a monastery hospital. Its ground plan shows rows of separate cells and a large stone trough used as a medicinal bath, serving a community reported to number about 2,000 monks. The ruins are dated to around the 9th century, and a 12th-century hospital at Polonnaruwa, where patients were immersed in herbal oil, more or less followed its plan. The *Mahavamsa* chronicle claims far more: that King Pandukabhaya built a lying-in house and a hall for the sick in the 4th century BCE. But it was composed around 500 CE, centuries later.

myth.tradition: Sri Lanka had public hospitals as early as the 4th century BCE, built by King Pandukabhaya.
myth.record: The 4th-century BCE lying-in house and hall for the sick are known only from the *Mahavamsa*, written about 900 years later. The Mihintale ruins themselves date from roughly the 8th–9th century CE.

links.note: An earlier Buddhist ruler's claim to have provided medical care.
The Christian charitable hospital, a parallel religious tradition.
Contemporary hospitals of the Islamic world.

title: The Four Tantras of Tibetan medicine

traditional.note: Tradition traces Tibetan medicine to the Buddha teaching as the Medicine Buddha, with an 8th-century physician, Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Elder, whom the Los Angeles County Museum of Art calls legendary.

confidence.note: Museum and scholarly sources credit the text to the 12th-century physician Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Younger, and scholars place the formation of the medical tradition between the 7th and 12th centuries. The sources do not say how much of the text he composed rather than gathered from earlier material, which is why the date is a range; the Buddha's authorship is religious tradition.

people: Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Younger (1127–1203), physician credited with the text
summary: One book underlies the medicine of Tibet, Mongolia, Bhutan and the Himalaya — and tradition says the Buddha himself dictated it.
body: The *rGyud bzhi*, or Four Tantras, is the single standard treatise on which Tibetan medicine rests, together with its Mongolian, Bhutanese and Himalayan offshoots. The medical tradition behind it took shape in Central Tibet between the 7th and 12th centuries out of Tibetan, Indian, Chinese, Persian and Central Asian knowledge. The text is credited to the physician Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Younger (1127–1203), honored as Tibet's physician king. Tradition tells a grander story, shown in a 1970 painting: one sage asks the Medicine Buddha to explain the Four Tantras and another recites the answers, and the book is written as their questions and answers.

myth.tradition: The Four Tantras are the Buddha's own teaching, handed down unchanged.
myth.record: This is religious tradition. The museum and scholarly sources here credit the text to Yuthok the Younger in the 12th century, and the medical tradition it serves drew on several earlier sources. An 8th-century Yuthok the Elder is described as legendary.

links.note: Indian medical learning, of which Vagbhata's work is a classic example, was one source Tibetan medicine drew on.
The classical Indian medical tradition behind part of the Tibetan synthesis.

title: Greco-Arabic medicine takes root in India

confidence.note: This was a slow transplantation rather than an event; Sultan Firuz Shah's own account documents a physician-staffed hospital in 14th-century Delhi. Later details, such as when the name *Unani* came into use, come from secondary accounts.

place: Delhi and other Muslim courts of northern India
people: Firuz Shah Tughlaq (born 1309), sultan of Delhi who endowed a hospital
Hakim Ajmal Khan, Delhi physician under whose aegis the Tibbia College was established
summary: A sultan's free hospital in Delhi, Persian doctors at the Mughal court, and a Greek-rooted medicine that is still taught across India.
body: Greek medicine, recast in Arabic and Persian, reached India with its Muslim rulers. At the Delhi Sultanate and the later Muslim courts, its physicians practiced *tibb* alongside Ayurvedic colleagues. In the 14th century Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq recorded that he endowed a hospital where physicians diagnosed the sick, regulated their diet and gave medicines at his expense, to "residents and travelers, gentle and simple, bond and free." The name *Unani*, "Greek," is first recorded only in the late 18th century; before that the medicine was simply *tibb*. It outlasted British rule: Hakim Ajmal Khan's Tibbia College in Delhi taught it outside the colonial system, and is state-recognized there today.

links.note: Avicenna's *Canon* was the premier medical text of the Islamic world on which Greco-Arabic medicine rested.
Endowed hospitals of the Islamic world; Firuz Shah's is a later Indian example.

title: Smallpox inoculation in Bengal

confidence.note: Holwell's printed account is firmly dated to 1767, and a Bengal vaccination official confirmed its outline in 1805. How long Bengalis had inoculated before that is undocumented.

people: J. Z. Holwell, Fellow of the Royal Society, author of the 1767 account
summary: Traveling Brahmin inoculators, a smallpox goddess and a strict diet: Bengal's way of beating smallpox as reported to London in 1767.
body: In 1767 J. Z. Holwell told London's College of Physicians how Bengal protected itself against smallpox. Every year, he wrote, small parties of Brahmin inoculators set out from religious colleges such as Benares to reach the villages before the smallpox season. Patients were prepared with a diet free of fish, milk and ghee; after inoculation, cold water was poured over their heads and offerings made to Sitala, goddess of smallpox. A vaccination official found the account still broadly accurate in 1805, though some details had changed. Holwell claimed the practice had "the sanction of remotest antiquity," but its real age is undocumented.

myth.tradition: Indian inoculation, or even vaccination itself, goes back thousands of years and was known in ancient India.
myth.record: No source cited here documents the age of Bengali inoculation; colonial writers' 'time immemorial' was a standard phrase for usage of unidentifiable origin. Supposed evidence that vaccination was known in ancient India was published in the *Madras Courier* in 1819, in what may have been conscious propaganda.

links.note: The Ottoman route by which inoculation reached England.
Vaccination later displaced inoculation in India, against resistance.

title: An Indian nose reconstruction reaches London

confidence.note: The *Gentleman's Magazine* letter of October 1794 survives and was reprinted by Carpue in 1816. Sources differ slightly on when the operation itself took place (the Science Museum says 1793; the letter says Cowasjee went more than a year without a nose after capture in 1792), and the operator is never named.

place: Near Poona (Pune), India; reported in London
people: Cowasjee, bullock driver with the British army and the patient
Thomas Cruso and James Findlay, Bombay surgeons the letter cites as having seen the operation performed
Joseph Constantine Carpue (1764–1846), London surgeon who adopted the method
summary: A mutilated bullock driver, a new nose cut from his forehead by a nameless craftsman near Poona, and a letter that rekindled interest in nose reconstruction in Europe.
body: In October 1794 London's *Gentleman's Magazine* printed a letter, signed only "B. L.," about a man named Cowasjee. A bullock driver with the British army in the war of 1792 against Tipu Sultan of Mysore, he had been taken prisoner and had his nose and one hand cut off. After more than a year without a nose he was given a new one by "a Mahratta surgeon, a Kumar" near Poona. Two Bombay surgeons, Thomas Cruso and James Findlay, were cited as having seen the operation performed.

A wax model of a nose was flattened and traced on the forehead. The skin was cut free except for a narrow bridge between the eyes, which kept its blood supply, then turned down and fixed to the stump. The letter said the operation was "not uncommon in India." Engravings of Cowasjee were published in London.

Europe had once had its own flap operations, from 16th-century Italy, but they had fallen out of use. In London, Joseph Constantine Carpue studied the reports, practiced on cadavers and in 1814 rebuilt an officer's nose; his 1816 book spread what became known as the Indian method. The Indian surgeon's name was never recorded.

myth.tradition: The Poona surgeon was performing Sushruta's ancient operation, handed down unchanged for two thousand years.
myth.record: The *Sushruta Samhita* describes a flap cut from the cheek, not the forehead. Nasal repair clearly had a long history in India, but how the 18th-century forehead method descended from the ancient text is undocumented.

links.note: The ancient Sanskrit text that describes nasal reconstruction with a cheek flap.
A later classical work that also describes the procedure.

title: From sarpagandha to reserpine

confidence.note: CIBA's 1952 isolation and launch of reserpine are well documented. Credit is contested: one scholarly account argues that earlier Indian work has been under-recognized, and the antiquity of the root's medical use is disputed.

place: Calcutta and Bombay, India; Basel, Switzerland
people: Gananath Sen, Calcutta physician trained in Ayurveda
summary: A root sold in Indian bazaars to calm the insane became, via Calcutta doctors and a Swiss firm, a blood-pressure pill and an early drug for psychosis.
body: The root of *Rauwolfia serpentina*, sarpagandha, was sold in Indian bazaars above all as a remedy for insanity. In 1931 two Calcutta physicians, Gananath Sen and Kartick Chandra Bose, reported that 20 to 30 grains of the powder twice daily calmed violent patients and lowered blood pressure. Rustom Jal Vakil's 1949 paper in the *British Heart Journal* drew Western attention to it, and in 1952 CIBA chemists isolated reserpine, sold as Serpasil for high blood pressure. Nathan Kline showed it worked in psychosis, and in 1957 he and Vakil won Lasker awards alongside chlorpromazine's pioneers.

myth.tradition: Reserpine is an ancient Ayurvedic drug, recorded in Indian texts for some 3,000 years.
myth.record: Sources disagree. One reviewer says the *Sushruta Samhita* mentions a root called sarpagandha, used against snakebite, though the plant was identified as *Rauwolfia* only centuries later. Bose wrote in 1932 that no drug matching it could be found in the classical Ayurvedic lexicons, and a 2018 review calls the 'Ayurvedic' label not entirely appropriate. Its use in bazaar and folk medicine is better documented.

links.note: The other early antipsychotic, honored alongside reserpine in 1957.
Unani physicians such as Hakim Ajmal Khan also prescribed the root.
